headline: US and Iran reignite their war over the Strait of Hormuz: Trump drops a 20% shipping fee but presses a naval blockade as strikes fly, pushing oil to a one-month high.
the_big_picture: The single thread running through today is the re-escalation of the US-Iran conflict at the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint that carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil. Trump backed off a threatened 20% transit fee but is pushing ahead with a naval blockade while both sides trade strikes and tankers come under attack, sending crude to a one-month high. That oil spike is the hinge for everything downstream: US inflation cooled to 3.5% but officials flagged fresh upside risk, India's inflation just breached its central bank's target, the rupee slid past 96 and the Sensex fell. Running underneath, an AI storyline cuts both ways: IBM shed roughly $70bn in a day after stumbling on AI deals, even as China's AI-driven exports jumped 27% and Nvidia began shipping powerful H200 chips into China.

stories.title: UN says nearly 500 Afghan civilians killed in Pakistan-Afghanistan border fighting since October
key_points: **499 civilians killed** and **1,216 wounded** in Afghanistan by cross-border fighting between **October and June**.
Pakistan blames Afghanistan for harboring the **Pakistani Taliban (TTP)**, a claim Kabul denies.
The deadliest single strike hit a **Kabul drug-treatment center** in March, killing hundreds.
Amnesty International says the Kabul strike should be investigated as a possible **war crime**.
The report documents cases of rescuers being hit by a **second strike** while pulling victims from rubble.
stories.background: Since the Afghan Taliban retook power in 2021, Pakistan has accused it of sheltering the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a separate militant group waging an insurgency inside Pakistan that is ideologically aligned with, but distinct from, the Afghan Taliban government. Kabul denies harboring the group. Tensions have hardened into open cross-border airstrikes and clashes over the past several months, tracked by the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA), the UN's human-rights monitoring body in the country.
stories.what_happened: UNAMA's latest human-rights report tallies casualties from cross-border fighting between October 2025 and the end of June 2026: 499 civilians killed and over 1,000 wounded on the Afghan side alone. The single deadliest incident was a Pakistani airstrike on a drug-treatment center in Kabul in March, which killed hundreds of civilians. The report also documents a pattern where rescuers digging through rubble after one strike were hit by a follow-up strike. Pakistan has not published its own civilian casualty count for fighting inside its territory.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a spiraling conflict between two unstable, nuclear-adjacent neighbors, driven partly by a militant group neither government fully controls, with a mounting civilian death toll on one side that so far has no accountability mechanism.
stories.ripple_effects: Continued fighting risks fresh waves of Afghan refugees toward Pakistan and Iran, further hardens Islamabad-Kabul relations at a moment both governments face internal instability, and complicates Pakistan's broader campaign against the TTP inside its own borders.
stories.why_now: This is the first comprehensive UN tally covering the fighting since it escalated last October, released as part of UNAMA's routine human-rights reporting.
stories.watch_next: Whether Pakistan releases its own casualty figures or disputes the UN count, and whether any ceasefire or diplomatic talks follow.

key_terms.definition: Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan — a militant group waging an insurgency against the Pakistani state, distinct from but ideologically linked to the Afghan Taliban government.
The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, the UN body that monitors and reports on human rights and civilian harm inside the country.

stories.the_lesson: In conflicts driven by non-state militant groups operating across a border, both governments can plausibly deny responsibility for civilian deaths — which is exactly why independent monitoring bodies like UNAMA matter.

stories.title: Global HIV funding drops 18%, UN agency warns of resurgence risk
key_points: Global HIV funding fell **18%** to just **$7.3 billion** in 2025 — the lowest level in nearly two decades.
**PrEP** uptake, the daily pill that prevents HIV, dropped **38%** across 62 reporting countries in a single year.
Community-led services for gay men and sex workers were cut by **82-85%** in a 47-country study.
UNAIDS warns of **6 million** more new infections and **4 million** more AIDS deaths over the next four years without new funding.
The **US previously supplied 75%** of international HIV funding before the Trump administration's 2025 cuts.
stories.background: For two decades, US funding through programs like PEPFAR anchored the global fight against HIV, paying for prevention drugs, testing, and community outreach across dozens of low-income countries. In early 2025 the Trump administration briefly halted all HIV-related foreign aid before partially restoring it, but most prevention programs — as opposed to emergency treatment — stayed curtailed. UNAIDS, the UN's dedicated HIV agency, has now published its first full-year accounting of the damage, timed to the 26th International AIDS Conference.
stories.what_happened: UNAIDS released a special report titled 'United to End AIDS' showing total global HIV funding fell 18% to $7.3 billion in 2025, the lowest level since the mid-2000s. A separate 47-country study found community-led HIV services for high-risk groups — gay men, sex workers, survivors of gender-based violence — collapsed by 72-85%. Funding for condoms was cut by more than 90% in some countries, and PrEP uptake fell 38% year-on-year across 62 countries. UNAIDS projects an additional 6 million infections and 4 million deaths over the next four years if the funding gap isn't closed.
stories.why_it_matters: Decades of steady progress against HIV — falling infections, falling deaths, near-normal life expectancy for people on treatment — depended on sustained funding that is now unwinding fast. The effects of a funding cut don't show up immediately; they show up years later as a resurgence.
stories.ripple_effects: Health systems in Africa and parts of Asia, which leaned hardest on US-funded programs, face the most immediate strain. Governments will have to choose between filling the gap domestically or accepting rising infection rates; either way, the cost of treating a resurgence later is far higher than the cost of prevention now.
stories.why_now: The report was timed to the International AIDS Conference (AIDS2026) and is the first complete year-over-year data since the 2025 US funding halt, giving the first clear picture of the damage.
stories.watch_next: Whether donor governments or the Global Fund announce new pledges at upcoming replenishment talks, and whether early infection-rate data starts ticking up in the hardest-hit countries.

key_terms.definition: Pre-exposure prophylaxis — a daily pill that prevents HIV infection in people who don't yet have the virus.
The US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, historically the largest single funder of global HIV programs.

stories.the_lesson: Cuts to prevention funding don't cause visible harm immediately — the damage shows up years later as new infections and deaths, which makes this kind of funding easy to cut and hard to defend in the moment.

stories.title: France orders 4,000 more evacuated as a fresh heatwave threatens to reignite the Bordeaux wildfire
key_points: French authorities evacuated **~4,000 more people** Tuesday from Atlantic coast tourist sites near Bordeaux.
The fire has burned **420 square kilometers** — an area **four times the size of Paris**.
Officials call the blaze **'stabilized, not fixed'**: unchanged overnight, but returning heat could restart its spread.
It has already forced roughly **330,000 people** to evacuate across France and Spain combined since last week.
stories.background: A wildfire west of Bordeaux, in France's Gironde region, has been burning since last week, at times turning into a self-feeding **firestorm** that outran containment efforts. It's part of a broader wave of wildfires across southwestern Europe, driven by a **heat dome** that has baked the region for days. Yesterday's coverage noted **over 360,000 people** had already fled homes and vacation lets across France and Spain, prompting French President Macron to call an emergency government meeting.
stories.what_happened: Firefighters held the Gironde fire in check through a calm night, containing flare-ups near coastal dunes and keeping the burned area steady at **420 square kilometers (162 square miles)**. But French authorities still ordered nearly **4,000 more people** evacuated Tuesday from tourist sites on the Atlantic coast, as rising heat and falling humidity threatened to undo that fragile hold. Officials described the fire as **'stabilized, not fixed'** — meaning it could flare up again as temperatures climb. Total evacuations from the France-Spain wildfire wave now stand at roughly **330,000 people**.
stories.why_it_matters: This shows how a wildfire can look 'under control' one day and be back in crisis the next once heat returns — firefighting gains are often temporary, not permanent, in a heatwave.
stories.ripple_effects: Continued evacuations disrupt the peak summer tourist season on France's Atlantic coast, hit local businesses, and add pressure on French and Spanish emergency services already stretched thin. Prolonged wildfire smoke and heat also strain public health systems and can damage crops and vineyards in the surrounding wine region.
stories.why_now: A new heat wave rolling back across southwestern Europe this week is the direct trigger for today's fresh evacuation order.
stories.watch_next: Whether the burned area holds at 420 sq km through this heat spell, or whether the fire escapes containment again.

key_terms.definition: A stubborn zone of high pressure that traps hot air over a region for days, pushing temperatures far above normal.

stories.the_lesson: A wildfire 'stabilized' is not a wildfire 'out' — as long as extreme heat persists, the risk of a fire reigniting stays live, which is why authorities keep evacuation orders active even after the immediate danger seems to pass.

thread.previously: Wildfires had already forced over 360,000 people to flee homes and vacation accommodation across southwestern France and Spain, prompting President Macron to call an emergency government meeting.
thread.changed: A fresh heatwave now threatens the fragile overnight containment near Bordeaux, prompting ~4,000 more evacuations even as the burned area itself held steady — officials call the fire 'stabilized, not fixed.'

stories.title: Israel and Lebanon set next round of Rome talks for August 4–6, building on their first troop pullout
key_points: The **next round of US-mediated talks** is set for **Rome, August 4–6**, a State Department official confirmed.
Talks will cover **expanding the pilot zone** in southern Lebanon and settling **border disputes**.
It follows the **successful launch of the first pilot zone**, where Lebanese Army troops replaced Israeli soldiers.
The push builds on the **14-point framework agreement** signed in Washington on **June 26**, which calls for Hezbollah's disarmament.
Lebanese President Aoun met Trump last week, which US officials called a source of **'significant momentum'**.
stories.background: Israel and Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militant group that controls much of southern Lebanon, fought an intense war in 2024 that devastated the border region. A **US-brokered framework deal** signed on **June 26, 2026** laid out a path to end the conflict for good: Hezbollah disarms, and Israeli troops leave in stages as the **Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF)** take over security. Since then, negotiators have met repeatedly in Rome to iron out the mechanics, focusing first on two small **'pilot zones'** north and south of the Litani River where the LAF has now taken over from Israeli soldiers as a proof of concept.
stories.what_happened: US officials confirmed that Israeli and Lebanese delegations will hold their next round of talks in Rome from **August 4 to 6**, at the same US Embassy venue used for prior rounds. The agenda: expand the pilot-zone model to more territory, resolve lingering border disputes, and move toward fuller implementation of the framework deal. A State Department official said the two sides are approaching the talks with **'significant momentum'**, citing the smooth handover of the first pilot zones and Lebanese President Joseph Aoun's meeting with President Trump last week. Even so, Israel's defense minister has told the Pentagon that Israeli troops will remain **indefinitely** in the broader security zones it holds across Lebanon, Syria, and Gaza — meaning full withdrawal is not imminent.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the most sustained diplomatic progress on the Israel-Lebanon border since the 2024 war, and a working model — swap Israeli troops for Lebanese ones, zone by zone — that could be replicated more broadly if it holds. But the gap between 'pilot zone handed over' and 'Israel actually leaves the wider security zones' is still enormous.
stories.ripple_effects: A durable Lebanon deal would remove one more active front in the wider Middle East conflict, alongside the Gaza ceasefire and the US-Iran de-escalation track — lowering the region's overall temperature and, with it, some of the risk premium in oil markets. Hezbollah's actual disarmament, if it happens, would also reshape Lebanon's fractured domestic politics, where the group is both a militia and a political party.
stories.why_now: This round was scheduled now because the first pilot-zone handover just went smoothly and Aoun's White House visit last week gave both sides political cover to keep going.
stories.watch_next: Whether the August 4–6 Rome round actually expands the pilot zones, or whether Israel's 'indefinite' stance on the broader security zones stalls things.

key_terms.definition: A small test area where a new arrangement — here, Lebanese Army troops replacing Israeli soldiers — is tried out before being rolled out more broadly.
A high-level deal that sets out the goals and broad steps both sides agree to, leaving the detailed mechanics to be negotiated afterward.

stories.the_lesson: Complex conflicts are rarely resolved in one signature — they're resolved zone by zone, meeting by meeting, with each small handover building (or breaking) the trust needed for the next one.
stories.market_link: A calmer Israel-Lebanon border reinforces the same de-escalation trade already pulling oil prices down alongside the US-Iran ceasefire.

stories.title: Drone strikes hit Sudan's El-Obeid hours after the army retook the city's lifeline highway

thread.previously: Sudan's army had just pushed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) off the 400-kilometre highway linking the capital Khartoum to El-Obeid — a rare battlefield win that raised hopes of relieving a city of roughly half a million people bracing for what aid groups warned could become a genocide-level siege, similar to the RSF's earlier atrocities in El Fasher.
thread.changed: Hours after that highway win, RSF drones struck El-Obeid anyway — a reminder that controlling a road doesn't end a siege that's increasingly being enforced from the air, and the city's fuel stations, power and water pumps are still failing.

key_points: **Drone strikes** hit El-Obeid on Monday, just hours after Sudan's army reclaimed the **400km highway** to Khartoum from the RSF.
More than **16 fuel stations** have been destroyed in El-Obeid, cutting power to the water pumps and bakeries that keep the city running.
Around **half a million people** are effectively trapped in the city as the RSF tries to enforce its dominance over North Kordofan state.
A disease outbreak has already killed **120 people** elsewhere in Sudan amid the broader collapse of health services.
Aid groups warn El-Obeid could become the next **El Fasher** — a reference to an earlier RSF siege that ended in mass killings.
stories.background: Sudan has been at war since April 2023 between the national army and the paramilitary **Rapid Support Forces (RSF)**, a conflict that has killed tens of thousands and displaced over 10 million people — one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. The RSF has besieged and stormed cities before; its capture of **El Fasher** in Darfur was accompanied by mass killings that the UN and rights groups have described as potential genocide. El-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, sits on a key highway link to Khartoum, making control of that road strategically vital for both sides.
stories.what_happened: Sudan's army spent days advancing across North Kordofan and, on Sunday, succeeded in pushing RSF fighters off the 400-kilometre highway connecting Khartoum to El-Obeid — reopening the city's main supply route. But the relief was short-lived: on **Monday**, drone strikes blamed on the RSF rocked El-Obeid itself, just hours after the highway was retaken. Residents have endured roughly a month of intense drone attacks and a near-total siege, during which more than **16 fuel stations** have been destroyed, cutting the power that runs the city's water pumps and bakeries. Around half a million people remain effectively trapped in the city. A disease outbreak — separate from the fighting — has already killed 120 people elsewhere in Sudan, compounding the crisis.
stories.why_it_matters: El-Obeid's fall or survival matters both for the half a million civilians trapped inside and as a signal of whether the RSF can be stopped from repeating the mass-killing pattern seen in El Fasher. Retaking a supply highway is a real military gain, but it doesn't neutralize drones — meaning the siege can continue by air even after the roads are secured.
stories.ripple_effects: A worsening siege would add to Sudan's refugee crisis, already one of the largest in the world, straining neighboring Chad, Egypt, and South Sudan. It also increases pressure on the African Union, UN, and G7 nations — which have already issued statements on El-Obeid — to intervene diplomatically or with aid access.
stories.why_now: The RSF's drone campaign is escalating precisely as the army notches a rare ground victory, suggesting the paramilitary group is shifting tactics from holding territory to punishing the city from the air when it can't hold the road.
stories.watch_next: Whether the army can also suppress RSF drone capability around El-Obeid, and whether humanitarian corridors open before fuel and water fully run out.

key_terms.definition: A paramilitary group fighting Sudan's national army for control of the country since 2023, accused of mass atrocities in Darfur.
Surrounding a city to cut off supplies like food, fuel and water, forcing surrender or causing a humanitarian collapse.

stories.the_lesson: Retaking territory on the ground doesn't end a modern siege if the attacker still controls the skies — drones let a weaker ground force keep strangling a city even after losing the roads around it.

stories.title: Nvidia in talks to guarantee $250 billion of OpenAI's mega Ohio data-center debt
key_points: Nvidia is negotiating a **$250 billion** guarantee so OpenAI can lease a giant **10-gigawatt** data-center campus SoftBank is building in Ohio.
Counting the Nvidia chips that would fill it, the whole project could cost more than **$500 billion** — one of the largest single AI infrastructure bets ever made.
Nvidia is separately discussing a further **$350 billion** financing package just to pay for the chips themselves.
The first phase, only **800 megawatts** of the planned 10 gigawatts, isn't due to finish until **2028** — this is a bet on AI demand years out, not today.
Nothing is signed yet: **terms are still being negotiated**, and the deal could still shrink or fall apart.
stories.background: Building the giant computer centers ('data centers') that run AI models like ChatGPT costs an enormous amount of money — for land, power supply, cooling, and above all the specialized chips (GPUs) that do the computing. **OpenAI**, the company behind ChatGPT, has committed to building far more computing capacity than it can currently afford outright, so it increasingly relies on its partners to help finance it. **Nvidia**, which makes most of the world's AI chips, has been doing exactly that: investing in and financially backstopping the very companies that buy its chips, including OpenAI and AI startup Safe Superintelligence. Critics call this 'circular financing' — money moving in a loop between a chipmaker and its customers — because it can make AI demand look stronger than it organically is.
stories.what_happened: The **Wall Street Journal** reported that Nvidia is in talks to provide a roughly **$250 billion** financial guarantee that would let OpenAI lease a planned **10-gigawatt** data-center campus in southern Ohio, being developed by SoftBank's energy arm. A guarantee like this effectively means Nvidia is promising to cover the debt if OpenAI can't, making it much easier for OpenAI to borrow the money in the first place. Beyond the guarantee, Nvidia is reportedly discussing a **separate $350 billion** financing arrangement specifically to fund the semiconductor chips that would go inside the facility. All-in, people familiar with the plan estimate the total project cost — land, buildings, power, and chips — could exceed **$500 billion**. Only the first phase, about 800 megawatts of capacity, is scheduled to be ready by **2028**; the full 10-gigawatt build-out would take much longer. As of the report, the deal terms were not finalized and could still change.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the largest financing arrangements in the history of the tech industry, and it deepens a web of mutual dependency between Nvidia and OpenAI — the chipmaker is effectively financing its own biggest customer's demand for its chips. If AI revenue growth doesn't keep pace with spending like this, the losses could ripple through Nvidia, OpenAI, and everyone who lent against these deals.
stories.ripple_effects: Nvidia's stock and the broader semiconductor sector tend to move on news like this — investors are increasingly asking whether **record AI capital spending** is translating into real, sustainable profits, or just inflating a bubble. It also raises power-grid demand questions for Ohio utilities, and puts pressure on rival chipmakers and cloud providers to match the scale of spending or risk falling behind.
stories.why_now: This surfaces just as investors are already jumpy about AI spending — South Korea's stock market recently tripped a circuit breaker on fears that AI-related capital expenditure has outrun the returns to show for it, so a fresh half-trillion-dollar commitment lands on an already nervous market.
stories.watch_next: Whether Nvidia and OpenAI actually finalize and disclose the terms of this guarantee in the coming weeks, and how markets react if they do.

key_terms.definition: A promise by one company to cover another's debt if it can't pay, which makes lenders more willing to lend in the first place.
A data center measured by how much electricity it draws — a 10-gigawatt facility would use roughly as much power as several large cities combined.
When a supplier invests in or funds its own customers, so money (and apparent demand) flows in a loop between a small number of related companies.

stories.the_lesson: When one company both supplies the product and finances the customer's ability to buy it, headline demand numbers can look stronger than the underlying economics really are — a pattern investors have been burned by before in other booms.
stories.market_link: Nvidia, OpenAI-linked private valuations, SoftBank, and the broader AI/semiconductor trade — this is exactly the kind of spending that's fueling both the AI rally and the AI-bubble fears investors are debating.

stories.title: Zelensky meets Britain's brand-new PM Andy Burnham aboard a Royal Navy carrier, wins fresh drone-jamming tech
key_points: Ukraine's President Zelensky met UK PM **Andy Burnham** aboard the carrier **HMS Queen Elizabeth** at Portsmouth.
It was Zelensky's visit — the **first by any foreign leader** since Burnham took office **a week ago**.
Burnham pledged new **'Stone Cloak' drone-jamming technology**, with thousands of units already delivered.
Talks focused on **ballistic-missile interceptors** to counter Russian strikes and joint defence production.
The meeting came a day **before Zelensky was due in Washington** to meet Trump.
stories.background: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched in February 2022, is now in its fifth year, and Ukraine remains heavily reliant on Western allies for air-defence equipment to shoot down Russian missiles and drones. The UK has been one of Kyiv's most consistent backers under successive governments. Andy Burnham became Britain's new prime minister only about a week before this meeting, making this Zelensky's first face-to-face test of where the new UK government stands on Ukraine.
stories.what_happened: On July 27, Zelensky travelled to Portsmouth Naval Base, where he met Burnham aboard the Royal Navy aircraft carrier HMS Queen Elizabeth — the first meeting between the two leaders and the first visit by any foreign head of state since Burnham took office roughly a week earlier. The two discussed joint drone projects, Ukraine's push for more ballistic-missile interceptors to counter Russian strikes, and closer joint defence production between the UK and Ukraine. Burnham announced the UK would supply new **'Stone Cloak' jamming technology** to protect Ukrainian drones from Russian jamming, on top of thousands of units Downing Street said had already been delivered. Burnham called the visit a signal of the UK's 'unwavering' support for Kyiv. The stop came one day before Zelensky's scheduled meeting with US President Trump in Washington.
stories.why_it_matters: A change of prime minister is often the moment allies get nervous about whether support will hold — this visit was Burnham using his very first foreign meeting to publicly commit to Ukraine, removing doubt about continuity in UK policy at a sensitive moment in the war.
stories.ripple_effects: The new jamming technology should make it harder for Russia to knock Ukrainian reconnaissance and strike drones out of the sky, a capability battle that has shaped much of the war's front lines. It also sets the tone heading into Zelensky's Washington meeting, where the bigger question — continued US military and financial backing — will be tested.
stories.why_now: Burnham took office only about a week ago, and hosting Zelensky first was a deliberate signal before he heads into wider diplomacy, including his own upcoming contacts with Washington and European partners.
stories.watch_next: What comes out of Zelensky's Washington meeting with Trump the next day, and whether the UK follows this visit with a broader package (funding or weapons) in the weeks ahead.

key_terms.definition: UK-supplied electronic jamming technology intended to shield Ukrainian drones from being jammed or tracked by Russian countermeasures.

stories.the_lesson: In alliance politics, the first meeting after a leadership change is a signal in itself — who a new leader chooses to host first, and what they promise, tells allies (and adversaries) whether a policy is going to hold or shift.
stories.market_link: Défense contractors tied to drone and jamming technology (UK and European) are a name to watch if the UK expands this kind of hardware commitment.

stories.title: Gunmen kill at least 30 in a midnight raid on Naridon village in Kaduna State
key_points: Gunmen attacked Naridon village around **11 pm on Sunday**, shooting residents and torching homes.
At least **30 people are dead, including 8 children**, with search teams fearing the toll could rise.
Nearby military posts were just **2 kilometres away** but reportedly did not respond during the hours-long attack.
Only **one soldier and four police officers** were stationed in the village after the killings.
The state government has ordered a **manhunt** and called the attack 'barbaric'.
stories.background: Naridon sits on the border between Kaduna and Plateau states, a stretch of central Nigeria known as the 'Middle Belt' where farming communities (mostly Christian) and herding communities (mostly Muslim Fulani) have clashed for years over land and water, a conflict often called the **Southern Kaduna crisis**. Armed groups — sometimes described as bandits, sometimes as militias — have repeatedly raided villages here with little warning and, residents say, little protection. Kaduna's state government has struggled for years to contain the violence despite repeated pledges of tougher security.
stories.what_happened: At around 11 pm on Sunday, July 26, gunmen invaded Naridon village in Kauru Local Government Area of Kaduna State, firing indiscriminately at residents before setting houses and shops ablaze. At least **30 people were killed, including 8 children**, and several more were injured; recovery teams warned the toll could climb further. The attackers reportedly operated for hours without being confronted. Residents said military units stationed roughly two kilometres away in nearby Kamaru and Ungwan Magaji did not arrive in time to stop the killing, and that only a single soldier and four Mobile Police officers were deployed to the community afterward. The Kaduna state government has condemned the attack and ordered security agencies to hunt down those responsible.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the deadliest single attacks in Nigeria's Middle Belt in months, and it underlines a pattern critics have raised for years: security forces stationed nearby but not reaching villages in time. For the families involved, it means sudden, mass loss of life in a region that had already been repeatedly targeted.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect renewed pressure on Nigeria's federal and Kaduna state governments to explain the security gap, and likely displacement as survivors flee to safer towns. Attacks like this also harden communal distrust between farming and herding communities, making local reconciliation efforts harder, and add to Nigeria's already heavy toll of conflict-driven displacement this year.
stories.why_now: The attack is the latest in a string of raids along the Kaduna-Plateau border in 2026, part of a longer-running cycle of communal violence that flares periodically when security deployments thin out.
stories.watch_next: Whether Kaduna state or federal authorities announce arrests or a beefed-up security deployment to the Kauru-Riyom border axis in the coming days.

key_terms.definition: The central region of Nigeria where farming and herding communities of different faiths live close together and have repeatedly clashed over land.

stories.the_lesson: A security force stationed 'nearby' isn't the same as protection — response time, not just troop numbers, decides whether a warning becomes a rescue or a headline about mass casualties.

stories.title: Israeli strikes kill 3 more Palestinians in Gaza, the latest breach of a ceasefire in name only
key_points: **3 Palestinians killed, 11 injured** in fresh Israeli strikes despite the ceasefire
Strikes hit **Jabalia, Deir al-Balah and near Al-Qarara Bridge** in different parts of Gaza
Since the ceasefire took effect in **October 2025**, over **1,200 more Palestinians** have been killed regardless
Israel controls roughly **70% of Gaza**, confining Palestinians to under a third of the strip
stories.background: A ceasefire in Gaza took effect on **October 10, 2025**, after nearly two years of war that followed Hamas's October 2023 attack on Israel. On paper, it was meant to stop major hostilities and let reconstruction and aid begin. In practice, Israeli strikes and Gazan casualties have continued at a lower but steady pace ever since, and Israeli forces still occupy a large majority of the territory.
stories.what_happened: Israeli drone and air strikes killed at least **three Palestinians** and injured **11 others**, in incidents in Jabalia, Deir al-Balah and near the Al-Qarara Bridge in southern Gaza. Local health officials say the ceasefire that began on October 10, 2025 has not stopped Israeli operations: more than **1,200 Palestinians have been killed** and nearly **3,900 injured** in the roughly nine months since it took effect. Israel's military maintains control over about **70% of Gaza's territory**, squeezing the population into less than a third of the strip. The pattern of near-daily strikes despite a nominal truce has become a recurring feature of the post-ceasefire period.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how a 'ceasefire' can exist on paper while the underlying violence continues at a reduced but real pace -- civilians in Gaza are still dying and being displaced even though the headline war has technically stopped.
stories.ripple_effects: Continued casualties keep regional tensions high and complicate any push toward a fuller, lasting peace or reconstruction effort. It also fuels criticism of the ceasefire's enforcement mechanisms from humanitarian groups and some governments.
stories.why_now: These are the latest in a long-running string of near-daily incidents since the ceasefire began, not a single dramatic escalation -- but each one adds to a toll that keeps climbing quietly.
stories.watch_next: Whether international mediators push for a tighter, better-enforced version of the ceasefire, or whether the current pattern of periodic strikes simply continues.

key_terms.definition: An agreement to stop major fighting, which doesn't always mean all violence stops -- as this case shows.

stories.the_lesson: A signed ceasefire is a political and diplomatic milestone, but it doesn't automatically mean fighting or casualties stop on the ground -- what happens after the agreement matters as much as the agreement itself.

stories.title: Zelensky's 30,000-more-troops claim meets Seoul's skepticism as North Korea's war role deepens

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's claim that Russia was trying to bring in another 30,000 North Korean troops for the Ukraine war, on top of the roughly 14,000-20,000 already deployed since 2024.
thread.changed: Today, South Korean government sources say they are watching the reports closely but have found no confirmed signs of a new deployment yet -- an official note of caution on Zelensky's claim -- while new reporting adds that Russia is also preparing to receive new North Korean ballistic missile launchers.

key_points: Zelensky says Russia is preparing space for **30,000 more North Korean troops** in its Voronezh region
That would **roughly triple** North Korea's current troop contribution to the war
**South Korea's own government** says it has no confirmed signs of a new deployment yet
Zelensky also says Russia is preparing to receive new **North Korean ballistic missile launchers**
stories.background: North Korea has backed Russia's war on Ukraine since 2024, when it first sent thousands of troops to help Russia retake territory in its own Kursk region after a surprise Ukrainian incursion. Around **14,000-20,000 North Korean soldiers**, including special forces and combat engineers, have been deployed to Russia so far, alongside artillery shells and missiles. In return, Pyongyang has reportedly gained battlefield experience for its army and technological help from Moscow. South Korea, the US and their allies see the arrangement as a serious escalation because it ties two adversaries closer together militarily.
stories.what_happened: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia is preparing to receive **30,000 additional North Korean troops**, with preparations under way since June in Russia's Voronezh region, close to the Ukrainian border. If it happens, this would **almost triple** North Korea's troop commitment beyond the roughly 14,000 currently believed to be serving with Russian forces. Zelensky added that Russia is also readying new North Korean ballistic missile launchers. South Korean government sources, however, say they are only tracking the reports and have **no confirmed evidence** yet that a new deployment is under way -- a notable gap between Kyiv's warning and Seoul's official caution.
stories.why_it_matters: A tripling of North Korean troops would be one of the largest foreign troop commitments to either side of the war and would further internationalize a conflict that started as a Russia-Ukraine dispute. It also deepens a security partnership that worries the US and its Asian allies, since North Korea gains real combat experience and Russian technology transfers in return.
stories.ripple_effects: If confirmed, a bigger North Korean deployment could ease pressure on Russia's own manpower shortages and let it sustain offensives for longer. It would also likely draw a sharper response from South Korea, Japan and the US, who already treat North Korea's missile and nuclear programs as a top security threat -- any battlefield-tested improvements Pyongyang brings home would concern them directly.
stories.why_now: Zelensky's warning comes as Russia keeps grinding forward in eastern Ukraine and looks for ways to sustain its offensive without a full domestic mobilization, making foreign troops an attractive option.
stories.watch_next: Whether South Korea's intelligence agencies confirm new North Korean troop movements toward Russia in the coming days.

key_terms.definition: A Russian region bordering Ukraine, used as a staging and training area for troops before they're sent to the front.

stories.the_lesson: In modern wars, official claims from one side (like Zelensky's) and independent confirmation from a neutral government (like Seoul's) can diverge -- a reminder to watch for corroboration before treating a wartime claim as settled fact.

stories.title: Sudan's Army Retakes Key Highway as El-Obeid Braces for a Possible Genocide-Level Siege
key_points: Sudan's army said it recaptured the **Al Sadarat highway** linking capital Khartoum to **El-Obeid** on Sunday, after two days of fierce fighting with the paramilitary **Rapid Support Forces (RSF)**.

El-Obeid, capital of North Kordofan state, has swelled to roughly **500,000** people as displaced Sudanese flee into it — and it remains besieged, with UN investigators warning it could become the next **El-Fasher**.

In just three weeks in June alone, the UN documented **15 drone strikes** on El-Obeid that killed at least **45 civilians**; drone strikes by both sides have killed over **1,000** people across the wider Kordofan region since January 2026.

A UN Fact-Finding Mission ruled on **July 9** that RSF's mass killings, gang rape and deliberate starvation during its 18-month siege of El-Fasher amounted to **genocide** against the non-Arab Zaghawa and Fur communities.
Food prices in besieged El-Obeid have surged by as much as **300%**, and residents say they can no longer afford to eat or to flee the city.
stories.background: Sudan has been at war since **April 2023**, when the regular army (SAF) split violently from its former partner, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), in a struggle for control of the country. The war has displaced more people than any other conflict on Earth and left around **5 million** Sudanese facing emergency or catastrophic hunger. Earlier this year the RSF captured El-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, after an 18-month siege marked by mass killings later ruled to be genocide by UN investigators — a precedent that has raised alarm that El-Obeid, Kordofan's regional capital, could suffer the same fate.
stories.what_happened: Sudan's army announced Sunday it had regained full control of the Al Sadarat highway, the main road linking Khartoum to El-Obeid, after driving out RSF fighters who had held it. The army said the operation inflicted heavy losses on RSF troops and forced them to retreat from towns along the route. Controlling the highway lets the army move troops, weapons, fuel and supplies into the besieged city and cuts off one of the RSF's main routes for pushing toward it. Even with the highway recaptured, El-Obeid remains encircled and under near-daily drone bombardment from both sides, striking markets, schools, water infrastructure and fuel stations. The UN's human rights chief, Volker Türk, has publicly warned that the city's civilians are being subjected to 'relentless' attacks as fears grow of a full RSF ground assault.
stories.why_it_matters: El-Obeid's roughly half a million residents face the realistic risk of a repeat of El-Fasher's genocide if the siege tightens into a full assault. The highway recapture is one of the Sudanese army's few recent battlefield successes and could buy the city time, but it does not end the siege or resolve the underlying war, now well into its third year with no peace deal in sight.
stories.ripple_effects: A worsening siege would push more refugees toward Chad, Egypt and South Sudan, straining already-overwhelmed regional aid systems and UN agencies that are severely underfunded for Sudan's crisis. Continued fighting in Kordofan also threatens Sudan's gold-mining regions and trade routes, further shrinking government revenue and prolonging the economic collapse driving the humanitarian emergency.
stories.why_now: The army's highway recapture happened Sunday (July 27) after two days of active battles, and UN officials are actively warning this week that the drone bombardment of El-Obeid is intensifying just as a ground assault looks increasingly likely.
stories.watch_next: Whether the RSF, cut off from the highway, launches a full ground assault on El-Obeid in the coming days, or whether the setback pushes it toward talks like the national dialogue proposed by Sudanese politician Malik Agar.

key_terms.definition: A paramilitary force that split from Sudan's army in 2023 and has since fought it for control of the country, accused by UN investigators of genocide in Darfur.
A military tactic of surrounding a city to cut off food, supplies and escape routes, forcing surrender or causing mass civilian suffering.
A formal determination, here by UN investigators, that violence was intended to destroy an ethnic or communal group 'in whole or in part' — the most serious legal label for mass atrocities.
People forced to flee their homes but who remain within their own country's borders, as opposed to refugees who cross into another country.

stories.the_lesson: Sieges on cities tend to follow a grim, predictable pattern — encirclement, bombardment, starvation, then either surrender or mass violence — which is why early warnings from human rights investigators about a city 'at risk of becoming the next X' deserve serious attention rather than being dismissed as speculation.

stories.title: AI Spending Fears Trigger Kospi Circuit Breaker as Samsung, SK Hynix Crash
key_points: South Korea's benchmark **Kospi** index plunged more than **8%** at the open, forcing the exchange to trigger a marketwide **circuit breaker** (an automatic 20-minute trading halt) at **10:13 a.m.** local time — the **8th** such halt in 2026 and the **14th** ever.
**Samsung Electronics** fell as much as **9.5–10%** and **SK Hynix** dropped up to **11–13%**, making them the two biggest losers in the entire **MSCI Asia Pacific** index, which fell about **3%**.
The **Kosdaq** (Korea's smaller-cap tech exchange) also fell over **8%** and triggered its own separate circuit breaker.
SK Hynix's US-listed shares had already closed overnight at **$143.02**, below their **$149** IPO price, after SanDisk sank **12%** and Micron dropped **5%** on Wall Street the prior session.

The panic followed China's memory-chip maker **CXMT** going public a day earlier and soaring as much as **530%**, becoming the world's 4th-largest DRAM maker and reviving fears it can undercut Samsung and SK Hynix on price.
stories.background: Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix together control roughly **65%** of the world's DRAM (computer memory chip) market, and their stocks have soared through 2026 on a wave of investment tied to the artificial intelligence boom — chips like theirs go into the servers that power AI systems like ChatGPT and Gemini. That rally has made Korea's Kospi index a global bellwether for whether investors still believe AI spending will pay off. China's CXMT, a state-linked memory maker, is racing to catch up and just listed its shares in Shanghai on July 27, instantly becoming China's most valuable listed company and stoking fears it will flood the market with cheaper chips.
stories.what_happened: On Tuesday, July 28, investors dumped Korean chip stocks the moment markets opened, sending the Kospi down more than 8% and forcing Korea Exchange to freeze all trading for 20 minutes at 10:13:43 a.m. — the third circuit breaker this month alone. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which together make up a huge share of the index's value, led the rout, both falling by double digits at their worst point. The Kosdaq saw an identical plunge and matching halt. The selloff had been building since Monday, when SanDisk, Micron and Western Digital all sank on Wall Street over the same worry: that hyperscalers' (the giant cloud companies like Microsoft, Google and Meta) massive AI data-center spending is running ahead of any proven payoff, and that CXMT's blockbuster IPO signals Chinese competitors can now undercut Korean and US memory makers on price. SK Hynix was due to report its second-quarter earnings the same day, adding extra volatility around the stock.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the sharpest sign yet that markets are losing confidence in the story that has driven global tech stocks for two years — that unlimited AI infrastructure spending automatically creates unlimited profits. Korea's chipmakers are critical suppliers to Nvidia and other AI hardware giants, so a crisis of confidence here signals doubt about the entire AI investment cycle, not just one country's stock market.
stories.ripple_effects: A sustained pullback in Samsung and SK Hynix share prices could slow their capital spending on new chip factories, tightening future memory supply. US chip suppliers (Micron, Western Digital, SanDisk) and AI-adjacent tech stocks on Wall Street are likely to see knock-on selling when US markets open, and other AI-exposed Asian markets (Taiwan, Japan) are watching closely. A cheaper, faster-than-expected Chinese entrant like CXMT could also pressure global memory prices lower over time, which would hurt margins across the whole industry, including US and Korean players.
stories.why_now: The circuit breaker fired live this morning (July 28) as part of an accelerating three-day selloff, right as SK Hynix reported earnings and a day after CXMT's record-breaking stock debut.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether SK Hynix's Q2 earnings report today reassures or further spooks investors, and whether US chip stocks (Micron, Nvidia, AMD) follow Korea lower when Wall Street opens.

key_terms.definition: An automatic, temporary halt in stock trading that exchanges trigger when prices fall too fast, meant to give investors time to calm down rather than panic-sell.
A type of memory chip used in nearly every computer and AI server to temporarily store data the processor is actively working with.
A giant cloud company (like Microsoft, Google, Amazon or Meta) that builds massive data centers, and is currently spending huge sums on AI chips and infrastructure.
A widely tracked basket of major Asian and Pacific stock markets, used as a barometer for the region's overall stock performance.

stories.the_lesson: When a whole industry's stock valuations rest on a single story — here, 'AI spending will keep paying off forever' — any credible challenge to that story, like a cheaper competitor emerging, can trigger outsized, fast market reactions even if the underlying business hasn't actually changed yet.
stories.market_link: Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are core holdings in most Asia-tech and semiconductor funds, so today's crash is likely to weigh on global chip and AI-related stocks, including US names like Nvidia, Micron and AMD, when Wall Street opens.

stories.title: DR Congo's Ebola outbreak tops 3,000 cases, spreading faster than any Ebola outbreak on record
key_points: Confirmed cases have passed **3,075**, with **1,354 deaths**, across **five provinces** of the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The outbreak hit **1,000 confirmed cases in just 40 days** — the 2018 North Kivu outbreak took **235 days** to reach the same mark.
Roughly **1,000 new cases were added in just the last 10 days**, prompting doctors to describe it as spreading '**like wildfire**.'
An angry mob **attacked a hospital in Nyakunde**, forcing Ebola patients and medical staff to flee, disrupting the response in the worst-hit province.
The virus has already **crossed borders**, with imported cases confirmed in Uganda, and travelers evacuated to Germany and France for treatment.
stories.background: Ebola is a severe, often-fatal viral disease spread through contact with bodily fluids of infected people; the strain driving this outbreak is the **Bundibugyo virus**, one of several Ebola-family viruses. The Democratic Republic of Congo has dealt with Ebola outbreaks before — including the 2018-2020 North Kivu outbreak, one of the worst in history — so the country has real experience and infrastructure for fighting it. This is the DRC's **17th recorded Ebola outbreak**, but responders say it is moving unusually fast: security problems in the eastern provinces, where armed groups operate and distrust of health workers runs high, have repeatedly disrupted containment efforts, including attacks on treatment centers and burial teams.
stories.what_happened: The Democratic Republic of Congo's health ministry has now confirmed more than **3,075 Ebola cases and 1,354 deaths** since the outbreak began, spread across five provinces including Ituri (the hardest-hit, with roughly 90% of cases) and North Kivu. Case numbers have accelerated sharply, adding about 1,000 new confirmed cases in just the ten days before July 27 — a pace doctors say outstrips prior DRC outbreaks. In mid-July, a crowd angered by a hospital death stormed the **Nyakunde hospital** in Ituri province, forcing Ebola patients and responding medical staff — including the aid group Samaritan's Purse — to flee, and some too-sick-to-move patients were left without treatment. The **UN peacekeeping mission (MONUSCO)** has since deployed a base near Nyakunde to help protect health workers going forward. The virus has also spread beyond DRC's borders: Uganda has confirmed 20 cases, and individual patients have been medically evacuated to Germany and France for treatment.
stories.why_it_matters: This is on pace to become one of the largest Ebola outbreaks ever recorded, and the security attacks on health responders are actively making it worse — a disease outbreak that could otherwise be contained is being amplified by violence and mistrust. Confirmed spread into a second country (Uganda) and evacuated cases reaching Europe show this is no longer a purely local containment problem.
stories.ripple_effects: Continued instability in eastern DRC could slow the medical response further, risking more cross-border spread into neighboring countries. International health bodies (WHO, CDC) and aid groups will likely increase funding and staff commitments, and countries near DRC may tighten travel or health screening measures if case growth continues at this pace.
stories.why_now: The outbreak crossed the symbolic 3,000-case mark in the days just before this report, and the Nyakunde hospital attack has become a flashpoint illustrating how insecurity is actively slowing the response.
stories.watch_next: Watch WHO's next situation report for whether the growth rate is slowing (as officials hoped after some signs of stabilization in Mongbwalu and Goma) or continuing to accelerate.

key_terms.definition: One of several distinct viruses in the Ebola family, first identified in Uganda in 2007; it causes the same severe hemorrhagic illness as other Ebola strains.

stories.the_lesson: Disease outbreaks aren't purely biological problems — how fast they spread often depends as much on trust, security, and whether responders can safely reach patients as it does on the virus itself.

stories.title: Trump and Netanyahu finally sit down at the White House, with Iran the make-or-break topic

thread.previously: We reported Netanyahu was departing Israel for Washington ahead of a tense Tuesday meeting with Trump, with the two leaders split over Iran policy — Netanyahu wanting to keep pressure on Tehran, Trump leaning toward the diplomatic off-ramp his own administration has been negotiating.
thread.changed: The meeting itself is now happening — Netanyahu landed in Washington and the two leaders sat down at the White House at 11 a.m. local time, away from cameras, with reports the visit almost didn't happen after Trump initially refused to meet until Israel made a Gaza-related concession.

key_points: Trump and Netanyahu met privately at the White House at **11 a.m. Tuesday**, their **first face-to-face talks in over five months**.
Iran topped the agenda, with Netanyahu wanting to keep military pressure on Tehran while Trump favors the **diplomatic track his team is already running**.
Trump reportedly **initially refused the meeting** until Israel made a **concession on Gaza**, according to Israeli press reports.
The talks also covered **Gaza's postwar order**, Lebanon and Syria security-zone withdrawals, and prospects for **Saudi-Israel normalization**.
Netanyahu traveled under **tightened security** over a reported Iranian threat, flying out of Nevatim Air Force Base rather than a commercial route.
stories.background: Israel and the US have been the closest of allies for decades, but the relationship between Trump and Netanyahu has been unusually strained through 2026 as the two disagree on how hard to press Iran after weeks of direct US-Iran strikes and counter-strikes. Trump's White House has separately been negotiating a **fragile ceasefire and Strait of Hormuz safe-passage arrangement with Iran**, a diplomatic track Netanyahu has been publicly skeptical of. This is their **first in-person meeting in more than five months** — an unusually long gap for two leaders whose countries are this tightly linked, and a sign of how much friction had built up beforehand.
stories.what_happened: Netanyahu flew to Washington for a scheduled 11 a.m. meeting with Trump at the White House on Tuesday, July 28 — held away from press cameras rather than in a public Oval Office session, a departure from Trump's usual style with visiting leaders. Israeli media reported that Trump had **initially refused the meeting** and only agreed after Israel signaled a concession on Gaza policy. The agenda centers on **Iran** — where Netanyahu wants continued military pressure and Trump prefers the negotiated track his administration has underway — plus the postwar plan for Gaza (including the stalled effort to dismantle Hamas), whether Israeli forces stay in security zones inside Lebanon and Syria, and the long-stalled push to expand the **Abraham Accords** to include Saudi Arabia. Netanyahu and his wife flew out of an Israeli air force base rather than a commercial airport, a precaution taken amid a reported security threat linked to Iran.
stories.why_it_matters: This meeting will shape whether the US-Iran ceasefire effort — including the delicate talks over safe passage through the **Strait of Hormuz**, a chokepoint for roughly a fifth of the world's oil — holds or collapses. Netanyahu pushing Trump toward renewed pressure on Iran, versus Trump sticking with diplomacy, is a fork in the road for the whole region's trajectory over the next few months.
stories.ripple_effects: Oil markets are already reacting to Iran-related headlines (prices fell nearly 7% on ceasefire progress reports the day before this meeting), so any sign the US-Iran track is fraying could send crude back up. A rockier US-Israel relationship also complicates the Gaza reconstruction plan and any Saudi normalization push, both of which need close US-Israel coordination to move forward.
stories.why_now: The meeting was locked in after days of pre-negotiation reported by Israeli outlets, and it lands right as the US-Iran ceasefire talks over the Strait of Hormuz are at a delicate, still-unresolved stage.
stories.watch_next: Watch for an official White House readout or joint statement after the meeting, and whether Iran's foreign ministry reacts to any shift in US posture.

key_terms.definition: A set of agreements starting in 2020 that normalized diplomatic relations between Israel and several Arab states; extending them to Saudi Arabia would be a major diplomatic prize.
A narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that a large share of the world's traded oil passes through — closing or restricting it can move global oil prices.

stories.the_lesson: When two allied leaders publicly disagree on strategy toward a shared adversary, the disagreement itself becomes a variable other countries and markets have to price in — it's not just what each side wants, but which side wins the internal argument.
stories.market_link: Oil prices are sensitive to any sign the US-Iran ceasefire track is strengthening or weakening — watch Brent/WTI crude in the hours after this meeting.

stories.title: The Fed's two-day meeting starts today — traders now think a rate hold is more likely than a cut
key_points: The **Federal Reserve's policy meeting runs July 28-29**, with a decision due Wednesday.
Markets now price roughly a **64% chance the Fed holds rates steady**, down sharply from an 87% chance just a week ago.
The Fed's target range has sat at **3.50%-3.75%** since its last move.
New Fed Chair **Kevin Warsh** has already changed how the Fed communicates — dropping traditional forward guidance for a **pure 'data-dependent' approach**, making each meeting harder to predict.
US inflation (CPI) rose **4.2% over the year to May 2026**, the biggest 12-month jump since April 2023 — well above the Fed's usual 2% comfort zone.
stories.background: The Federal Reserve is the US central bank — it sets the short-term interest rate that ripples through mortgages, credit cards, business loans, and, because the US dollar and Treasury market are the anchor of global finance, borrowing costs worldwide including in India. Earlier this year the Fed brought in a new chair, Kevin Warsh, who has shifted the Fed's style: instead of pre-signaling what it plans to do next ("forward guidance"), the Fed now says it will decide meeting-by-meeting based purely on incoming data. That makes each Fed decision, including this one, more of a genuine toss-up for markets than it used to be.
stories.what_happened: The Fed's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) — the group of officials who set US interest rates — began its scheduled two-day meeting today, with the rate decision due tomorrow, July 29. Going into the meeting, futures markets (where traders bet on what the Fed will do) put the odds of a **hold at rates unchanged around 64%**, a sharp shift from just a week earlier when a hold looked far more certain at 87%. That shift reflects genuine uncertainty: inflation is running hot, with the Consumer Price Index up **4.2% year-over-year through May 2026** — the sharpest annual rise since April 2023 — which normally argues for the Fed to keep rates high or even raise them. But there are also signs of a softening labor market pulling in the opposite direction, toward a cut. The rate has held at **3.50%-3.75%** since the last change, and Warsh's shift away from forward guidance means officials aren't tipping their hand before Wednesday.
stories.why_it_matters: The Fed's rate decision is one of the single biggest swing factors for global markets — it affects how expensive it is to borrow everywhere, how attractive the US dollar is versus other currencies (including the rupee), and how much money flows into or out of emerging markets like India. A surprise cut or hold can move stocks, bonds, gold, and currencies worldwide within minutes of the announcement.
stories.ripple_effects: If the Fed holds rates steady with hawkish (inflation-focused) language, expect the dollar to strengthen and pressure on emerging-market currencies like the rupee, plus higher US Treasury yields pulling money away from riskier assets. If it leans toward signaling a future cut, expect the opposite — a weaker dollar, rally in gold, and relief for import-heavy economies. Indian markets, which already moved on Fed-adjacent oil and rate expectations this week, will be watching closely.
stories.why_now: This is a regularly scheduled meeting (the Fed meets roughly every six weeks), but it's landing at an unusually contested moment — hot inflation data pulling one way, a wobblier jobs picture pulling the other, and a new Fed chair whose communication style has made the outcome genuinely unpredictable rather than pre-telegraphed.
stories.watch_next: The rate decision and Chair Warsh's press conference on Wednesday, July 29, including any language about the path for the rest of 2026.

key_terms.definition: The group of US Federal Reserve officials who meet roughly every six weeks to set the US interest rate.
When a central bank tells markets in advance roughly what it plans to do at future meetings, so there are fewer surprises — the new Fed chair has moved away from this.
A measure of how much prices for everyday goods and services have risen — the most-watched gauge of inflation.

stories.the_lesson: When a central bank stops giving forward guidance and goes fully 'data-dependent,' every fresh economic report becomes a market-moving event on its own — traders can no longer coast on a pre-announced plan, so volatility around each data release tends to rise.
stories.market_link: US Treasury yields, the dollar index, gold, and — via capital flows — Indian equities, the rupee (USDINR), and RBI's own rate path all react to this decision.

stories.title: US and Iran edge toward a formal ceasefire deal, with the Strait of Hormuz the last sticking point
key_points: Mediators report **real progress** reviving talks after nearly two weeks of direct US-Iran fighting.
The sketched compromise would let Iran manage ship traffic through the **Strait of Hormuz** with **fewer restrictions**, instead of the US demanding open access outright.
President Trump says Washington paused renewed strikes **at Iran's request**, but warns they resume if no deal is reached.
Iran's Foreign Ministry publicly denies any active negotiations are underway — the two sides are not yet aligned on the basic facts.
Even with a pause, Iran-backed militia drones are still flying: **Saudi Arabia shot down drones** fired at it from Iraq this week.
stories.background: In early July 2026, a rapid escalation between the US and Iran turned into the most direct fighting between the two countries in decades, with US strikes on Iranian targets and Iranian retaliation that spilled into the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which **about a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments pass** every day. Iran responded to strikes by asserting more control over the strait and firing on vessels, which is what sent oil prices spiking and then, on hopes of a ceasefire, tumbling nearly 7% (as covered here yesterday). A truce has technically been holding for over a week, but the two sides have not yet signed anything formal.
stories.what_happened: Regional mediators say they've made genuine headway getting US and Iranian officials back to the table after the fighting paused. The emerging shape of a deal centers on the Strait of Hormuz: rather than Iran ceding full control, it would be allowed to **run vessel-transit management through the strait with fewer restrictions on ships** than the US originally wanted — a face-saving compromise for Tehran. President Trump said the US held off on resuming strikes **because Iran asked it to**, while making clear the US remains ready to hold Iran to account if talks collapse. Muddying the picture, Iran's Foreign Ministry told reporters there are **no current negotiations** taking place — a direct contradiction of the mediators' account. Meanwhile the ceasefire remains fragile in practice: Saudi Arabia intercepted and shot down drones this week fired by Iran-backed militia groups operating out of Iraq, a reminder that the wider network of Iran-aligned armed groups across the region hasn't stood down.
stories.why_it_matters: The Strait of Hormuz is the world's most important oil chokepoint — a real disruption there doesn't just hurt Iran or the US, it moves fuel prices everywhere, including at the pump in India. Whether this ceasefire becomes a real, signed deal or quietly falls apart determines whether that risk stays elevated through the rest of 2026.
stories.ripple_effects: Oil markets are trading on ceasefire headlines almost daily — expect continued volatility in crude prices, and knock-on moves in Indian fuel costs, airline stocks, and inflation forecasts. A durable deal would also ease pressure on global shipping insurers and Gulf state economies; a collapse would risk another spike like the one seen two weeks ago.
stories.why_now: The contradiction between the mediators (who say talks are progressing) and Iran's own Foreign Ministry (which denies any negotiation) is surfacing today because both sides are under pressure to show their own domestic audiences they haven't caved — Iran doesn't want to look like it's negotiating from weakness, while the US wants credit for de-escalating.
stories.watch_next: Whether Iran's Foreign Ministry statement is contradicted or confirmed by an actual signed framework in the coming days — and whether the Strait of Hormuz stays open to shipping without incident.

key_terms.definition: A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments must pass through — control over it means control over a huge share of global energy supply.
An agreement to stop fighting, which can be informal and shaky (like this one) or later formalized into a signed, binding deal.

stories.the_lesson: In a conflict over a chokepoint like Hormuz, an informal pause in fighting is not the same as peace — prices and markets stay jumpy until there's an actual signed agreement, because a single contradicting statement from either side can undo weeks of de-escalation.
stories.market_link: Crude oil prices (Brent/WTI), Gulf shipping and insurance names, and Indian oil-marketing companies (which import heavily via Hormuz) all move on ceasefire headlines here.

thread.previously: Yesterday, oil prices sank nearly 7% as the ceasefire held and Tehran opened talks on the Strait of Hormuz, with early signs the two sides were moving toward de-escalation.
thread.changed: Today mediators say real progress is being made on a Hormuz vessel-transit compromise, but Iran's own Foreign Ministry is publicly denying any negotiations are happening — and Saudi Arabia just shot down Iran-backed militia drones, showing the ceasefire is still fragile on the ground.

stories.title: Deportation protections for 300,000+ Haitians in the US expire today, and ICE is ready to move
key_points: A federal appeals court's temporary block on ending **Temporary Protected Status (TPS)** for Haitians expires **today, July 27**, clearing the way to strip protections from roughly **300,000 Haitians**.
ICE has been preparing targeted enforcement operations, including in **Ohio**, home to a large Haitian community, with deportation flights reportedly able to begin within days.
The **US Supreme Court** already ruled on **June 25** that the administration could proceed with ending TPS for Haiti and Syria, so today's deadline is the last of three court-ordered delays.
Roughly **145,000** of the affected Haitians live in Florida, including about **36,000** working in health care.
Migrants who leave voluntarily can be offered a government-funded flight home plus a **$2,600** payment.
stories.background: Temporary Protected Status lets people from countries hit by war, disaster, or crisis live and work in the US legally, without a path to citizenship, as long as their home country's designation stays active. Haiti has held TPS for over a decade because of gang violence, political collapse, and a 2021 earthquake that made large parts of the country unsafe to return to. The administration moved to end Haiti's TPS status earlier this year, arguing conditions no longer justify it — a decision challenged in court as endangering people who fled genuine danger. The Supreme Court sided with the administration on **June 25**, but a federal appeals court kept issuing short extensions, pushing the deadline back three times, with today marking the final one's expiry.
stories.what_happened: The US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit's temporary block on revoking Haitian TPS status expires today, after the court pushed the deadline back multiple times since late June while weighing the government's case. Unless a last-minute order intervenes, roughly **300,000 Haitians** living legally in the US under TPS lose that protection and their work permits starting today. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been preparing targeted operations to arrest and deport Haitian migrants, according to internal documents reported by CBS News, with Ohio — home to a large Haitian population in cities like Springfield — identified as an early target. The Supreme Court already cleared the way for this on **June 25**, in a ruling that also stripped protections from about 6,000 Syrians, so today's expiry is procedural rather than a new legal decision. Affected migrants can accept a government-funded flight and a $2,600 payment to leave voluntarily, or risk arrest and forced deportation. An estimated 145,000 of the affected Haitians live in Florida alone, including roughly 36,000 in health care roles.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the largest single removals of legal status from any immigrant group in recent US history, affecting people who have built homes, jobs, and families in the US for years under a legal program. It also lands on a country many experts say remains genuinely unsafe — Haiti has had no functioning elected government for years and large parts of its capital are controlled by armed gangs.
stories.ripple_effects: US industries that rely on Haitian TPS workers — healthcare, meatpacking, construction — face sudden labor shortages in the communities where they're concentrated, like Springfield, Ohio and South Florida. Haiti itself must absorb a wave of returnees with few jobs or services waiting for them. The move also sets a template for how the administration may treat other countries' TPS holders, including Venezuelans and Hondurans, whose protections face similar legal fights.
stories.why_now: Today is simply the date the courts set — the third and final deadline the DC Circuit granted before its temporary block on the Supreme Court's June ruling runs out.
stories.watch_next: Whether ICE moves quickly on the reported Ohio operations in the coming days, and whether Haitian advocacy groups win any further emergency stay.

key_terms.definition: A US immigration status that lets people from designated crisis-hit countries live and work legally in the US without a path to citizenship, renewed periodically by the government.

stories.the_lesson: A Supreme Court ruling doesn't end a legal fight immediately — lower courts can still grant short delays, so the actual deadline date, not just the headline verdict, is what determines when a policy truly takes effect.

stories.title: Houthi drones strike Saudi Arabia's main east-west oil pipeline, widening the Yemen war's reach into the kingdom's oil backbone
key_points: Yemen's Houthi rebels launched drone strikes today targeting Saudi Arabia's **Petroline**, the pipeline that carries **7 million barrels a day** from eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the strikes hit pumping and transport points, calling it retaliation for **repeated Saudi drone incursions into Yemeni airspace**.
Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Defense said its air defenses **intercepted and destroyed** the attacking drones before any damage.
It follows Houthi strikes on Aramco refineries in **Jizan and Yanbu** days earlier that sent Brent crude above **$100 a barrel**.
The Houthis have also declared a **naval blockade** of Saudi ports this month, marking a sharp escalation from the years-long truce.
stories.background: Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement held an uneasy truce for several years after a brutal civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis seized Yemen's capital Sanaa and a Saudi-led coalition intervened to back the internationally recognized government. That truce unraveled this month after a Saudi strike on Sanaa's airport aimed at stopping an Iranian plane from landing, provoking the Houthis into firing missiles at Saudi Arabia and declaring a **blockade** of its ports. The Houthis are part of Iran's regional network of allied armed groups, and their return to open conflict has opened a new front in the wider **US-Israel-Iran confrontation** that has dominated the region this year. Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure was last hit at this scale roughly four years ago.
stories.what_happened: On Monday, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched drone strikes on facilities along Saudi Arabia's East-West crude pipeline, known as Petroline, which moves oil roughly 1,200 km from the kingdom's eastern fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. The pipeline normally runs at its full capacity of **7 million barrels a day** and exists partly so Saudi Arabia can export oil without routing tankers through the Strait of Hormuz. Saree said the attack targeted supply and transport points, framing it as retaliation for repeated Saudi drone flights over Yemeni territory. Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Defense confirmed its air defenses intercepted and destroyed several drones, with no reported casualties or disruption to pipeline flows. This is the third major Houthi strike on Saudi oil infrastructure within a week, after attacks on Aramco's Jizan and Yanbu refineries on July 25 briefly pushed Brent crude above $100 a barrel. Shipping through the nearby Bab el-Mandeb Strait has already fallen to its lowest level in months as vessels avoid the area.
stories.why_it_matters: Petroline exists specifically so Saudi Arabia isn't fully dependent on shipping oil through the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has threatened to close before. If the Houthis can credibly threaten that pipeline too, Saudi Arabia loses its main insurance policy against a Hormuz shutdown — which is why even an intercepted, damage-free strike moves oil markets.
stories.ripple_effects: Sustained attacks raise insurance costs for tankers and pipeline operators, which eventually shows up in fuel prices worldwide. It also pulls Saudi Arabia further into a war it had tried to stay out of since 2022, raising the risk of broader Saudi-Houthi and Saudi-Iran escalation. For India, which imports over 80% of its crude, sustained Gulf instability directly affects fuel costs, inflation, and the rupee.
stories.why_now: The truce that had held for roughly three years collapsed this month after the Saudi strike on Sanaa airport, and the Houthis have escalated in stages since — missiles, a naval blockade, refinery strikes, and now a direct hit on the pipeline that is Saudi Arabia's oil lifeline.
stories.watch_next: Whether Saudi Arabia responds militarily against Houthi positions in Yemen beyond its July 25 airstrikes on Hodeidah.

key_terms.definition: A roughly 1,200-km pipeline carrying Saudi crude from eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, letting the kingdom export oil without sailing tankers through the Strait of Hormuz.
A Yemeni armed political movement, backed by Iran, that controls much of northern Yemen including the capital Sanaa and has fought a Saudi-led coalition since 2014.

stories.the_lesson: When a country builds a backup route for something as critical as oil exports, that backup becomes a target the moment tensions rise — redundancy only protects you until an adversary can reach the redundant path too.
stories.market_link: Brent and WTI crude typically jump on Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure; watch energy stocks, Indian oil-marketing companies exposed to crude swings, and the rupee, which weakens when India's import bill rises.

thread.previously: Houthi strikes on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea sent Brent crude above $100 a barrel for the first time since May, before prices eased back to around $97-98 by July 24.
thread.changed: The Houthis have now struck Saudi Arabia's main East-West pipeline directly rather than tankers at sea — hitting fixed oil infrastructure inside Saudi territory, though Saudi air defenses say they intercepted the drones this time.
